answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
The overall proposed approach misaligns with the approach the existing Scope 2 TWG subgroup has actually been developing over recent months. To learn more about this misalignment and ways to substantially improve the unusable and ineffective consequential method published for this public consultation, review the Marginal Impact Method’s public statement via https://marginalimpactmethod.org/.

From EPP’s perspective, an Emissions Impact-based Method (EIM) should be (re)integrated with Scope 2 accounting. EIM would reflect the differentiated decarbonization impact of procuring a given EAC in a particular place and time. It would offer a straightforward approach and new incentive for companies to procure clean energy to address their Scope 2 emissions wherever the highest impact EAC is available (i.e., in the most carbon intensive places using a global boundary).

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The overall proposed approach misaligns with the approach the existing Scope 2 TWG subgroup has actually been developing over recent months.

Introducing a new impact metric as a third ledger within Scope 2—such as an Emissions Impact-based Method (EIM)—would provide a critical accounting pathway for highest-ambition corporate strategies that optimize for global decarbonization impact and energy access expansion. The impact metric would still rely on MWh matching and use EACs. What would be new is the introduction of grid carbon intensity to reflect the differing impact of buying one EAC versus another EAC. Each EAC would retain the standard zero emission factor, but would vary based on the average and marginal emission factors of the time and place where the MWh underpinning the EAC was generated. This would incentivize companies to procure more EACs in the places and times where the grid is the most carbon-intensive to support more investments in clean energy in those places and times.
To better understand how this could be implemented in reality, imagine two similar companies—Company A and Company B—that have identical geographic distributions of global electricity consumption and both have 100% clean energy procurement targets. In both cases, these two companies bought clean energy 100% matching their annual volume and have the relevant EACs for each MWh of clean energy they bought. Company A pursued the traditional approach to geographic matching, only buying clean energy from the same national or regional market as its consumption and matching 100% annually. Company B, however, pursued an emissions-first approach and procured clean energy with 100% volume match where some of its procurement occurred outside of its market boundary for procurement options in more carbon-intensive markets. In this case, under existing GHG Protocol Scope 2 guidance, Company A would report a better market-based number and report “zero” given its 100% clean energy volume match. Company B would, however, perform less well under the market-based method than Company A, but would perform better than Company A with the emissions impact-based method. This is because Company B would have EACs from markets with higher national average and/or marginal emissions, so Company B’s carbon-intensity per EAC procured would be higher—meaning it sent stronger demand signals for clean energy in more carbon-intensive places than Company A did.
Ideally, the market-based method will change to allow conditional out-of-market procurement for clean energy from more carbon-intensive and under-electrified regions so that Company B would also report “zero” market-based emissions for achieving its 100% annual clean energy volume match in addition to reporting stronger emissions impact under the proposed new Scope 2 EIM.
Introducing a new impact metric would resolve tension between maintaining inventory integrity and enabling/incentivizing highest-impact corporate action focused on decarbonization impact. It would allow Scope 2 to maintain rigor around directly attributable emissions with MWh-based matching while complementary metrics capture broader system impacts that are currently invisible in accounting frameworks.
The new metric would be particularly valuable for accounting for:
Increased energy access and clean energy leapfrogging in under-electrified regions
Procurement optimized for average and/or marginal emission reductions within or outside an organization’s local market
Long-term agreements supporting new project development in more carbon-intensive regions as well as more carbon-intensive times of day / months of the year in a given location
This approach aligns with principles of completeness (accounting for all relevant corporate actions in all markets), relevance (supporting decision-making for highest-ambition strategies), feasibility (grid carbon intensity and marginal emissions data are, unlike hourly data, already accessible), and consistency.

Please find EPP’s detailed concerns about potential new hourly deliverability requirements, proposed alternative and preferred revisions to Scope 2 MBM to enable higher-ambition corporate strategies (including details on how to implement an Emissions Impact-based Method (EIM), and a full list of existing categorized research resources in the formal appeal that EPP submitted to GHG Protocol in June 2025 (via https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5cc327c55acb9b00019d816a/t/68506e46aa2d0a60741432c6/1750101575718/EPP+Appeal+Letter+to+GHG+Protocol+Secretariat+%26+ISB+-+June+2025.pdf ) and summarized in an accompanying blog (via https://www.energypeacepartners.com/blog/epps-appeal-for-complete-scope-2-guidance ).

EPP submitted this appeal to the GHGP’s ISB and Secretariat in June 2025, which built on letters EPP submitted to the Secretariat previously in 2024.
